2026-11-10-body-02.description:
In a vacuum you don't explode, because your tissue is strong enough. Water boils at body temperature, so wet spots like your eyes and mouth go first, and NASA astronaut-physician Michael Barratt puts useful consciousness at about 12 seconds. In December 1966, NASA test subject Jim LeBlanc's suit hose came loose in a Houston vacuum chamber. He felt his saliva boil off his tongue before passing out, and the chamber was repressurized. He had no long-term effects.

2026-11-10-body-03.description:
A hiccup is a spasm of your diaphragm, the muscle below your lungs, followed by your vocal cords snapping shut: that's the "hic". Most bouts last a few minutes; hiccups lasting more than 48 hours are called persistent, and Cleveland Clinic and the NHS say to see a doctor if they go past two days. Experts haven't found a proven hiccup cure. Charles Osborne started hiccuping after a fall while hanging a hog in 1922 and didn't stop until 1990: 20 to 40 times a minute, an estimated 430 million hiccups. He married twice and had eight children.

2026-11-10-body-04.title: What Happens When You Get Brain Freeze?
2026-11-10-body-04.pinned_comment: What gives you the worst brain freeze: ice cream, a slushie, or ice water? Did the tongue trick work for you?

2026-11-10-body-04.description:
Brain freeze (scientific name: sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia) starts when something cold, like ice cream, suddenly chills the roof of your mouth. Your body tries to warm up: blood vessels in your head change size to let in extra blood, and the trigeminal nerve, which carries pain from your face, sends the signal. You feel it in your forehead and temples instead of your mouth. It's not serious and usually lasts a few seconds to two minutes. To help it pass, press your tongue or thumb against the roof of your mouth, or sip something warm or room temperature.

2026-11-10-body-05.description:
Goosebumps (piloerection) are an automatic reaction of your sympathetic nervous system, your fight-or-flight mode. Tiny muscles at the base of each hair follicle (the arrector pili) contract, so the hairs stand up and small bumps form. Cold, fear, shock, excitement and even music or a movie can set them off. In animals it makes them look bigger, like a cat that puffs up while it hisses; in humans it mostly helps conserve a little heat. A 2020 Harvard study in mice suggests a second job: the same nerve, bridged by that muscle, wakes up hair follicle stem cells, and mice kept in the cold grew new hair in under two weeks.

2026-11-10-body-06.description:
That "asleep" feeling is temporary paresthesia: sitting with your legs crossed too long puts sustained pressure on a nerve (body position can also limit blood flow), so the messages between your foot and your brain get interrupted and the foot goes numb. Move, the pressure is released, and the nerve "wakes up": that's the pins and needles, a tingling, prickling or burning feeling that fades in a minute or two with no permanent damage. If it won't go away or happens often, see a doctor.

2026-11-10-body-07.description:
A knocked-out adult tooth put back in its socket, or stored properly, within five minutes will likely survive. Hold it by the crown, never the root: the root carries tiny fibers it needs to heal. Don't scrub it or put it in water. If it won't go back in, keep it in milk or your own saliva and get to a dentist or emergency department right away. Baby teeth are not put back.

2026-11-10-body-08.description:
A narrow passage called the eustachian tube links each middle ear to the back of your nose and throat. It stays shut until you swallow, yawn or chew; then it opens, air gets in, and the pressure on both sides of your eardrum evens out. On a plane the pressure can change faster than the tube can adjust, so hearing goes muffled. If ear discomfort, fullness or muffled hearing lasts more than a few days, or is severe, see a doctor.

2026-11-14-body-01.description:
A charley horse is a muscle cramp: a sudden tightening, most often in the calf, where the muscle contracts on its own and can't relax. It can last from a few seconds to 10 minutes, and most people get them at night or while resting. Stretching and massaging the muscle, or putting your weight on that leg, may ease it, and the muscle can stay sore afterward. See a doctor if cramps happen often, are severe, or come with swelling or numbness.

2026-11-14-body-02.description:
Tears are made by glands behind the upper outside corner of each eye. Every blink drains used tears into your tear ducts, which empty into the back of your nose. When you cry, tears flow in faster than usual and drain into your throat, which is why you might feel stuffy after crying. Emotional tears, triggered by feelings like sadness or joy, contain more stress hormones and natural painkillers than everyday tears.

On darker skin it can look slightly darker instead of red, and if an emotion caused it, it may go away once you relax.

2026-11-14-body-04.description:
Motion sickness happens when your eyes, inner ear and body send your brain conflicting messages: your eyes sense movement while your inner ear senses you're sitting still. Symptoms can include dizziness, nausea, a cold sweat and salivating more than usual, and it's more likely to affect kids ages 2 to 12 than adults. Looking at the horizon, facing forward and getting fresh air can help.

2026-11-15-body-02.description:
The most common cause of nosebleeds is dry air: it dries out the delicate tissue inside your nose until it gets crusty or cracked, and the tiny blood vessels there lie close to the surface. Most nosebleeds start at the front of the nose and usually aren't serious. To stop one, sit down, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose just above your nostrils for 10 to 15 minutes while breathing through your mouth. If it lasts longer than that, get emergency help, and don't drive yourself.

Most providers call it a fever at 100.4 F (38 C). It happens when your brain's thermostat resets to a higher temperature, mostly in response to an infection, and many people feel chilled when they have one. Adults should call a healthcare provider if a fever goes above 103 F (39.4 C) or lasts longer than about three to four days.

2026-11-15-body-04.description:
Ultraviolet rays from the sun burn your skin, and the damage to the DNA in your skin cells is permanent. Your skin's blood vessels widen, which causes redness and swelling, and the pain usually starts within a few hours and peaks around 24 hours. Peeling usually starts a few days later: new skin layers grow underneath and the dead outer layer peels away, but that dead layer still protects the new skin, so don't pick it. Cool showers, aloe and plenty of water help. Get urgent medical advice if your skin is blistered or swollen, or you get chills.

2026-11-16-body-01.description:
Send this to the friend who whispers all day when they lose their voice.
Laryngitis is when your voice box or vocal cords become irritated or swollen, usually from a virus like a cold, but yelling and overusing your voice can do it too. Swollen cords can't vibrate properly, so your voice goes hoarse or disappears. The NHS says to speak as little as possible and not to talk loudly or whisper, because both strain your voice, and to drink plenty of fluids. It usually clears up on its own within 1 to 2 weeks; see a doctor if it hasn't improved after 2 weeks or keeps coming back, and get urgent help if it's very painful to swallow or hard to breathe.

2026-11-16-body-02.description:
Send this to the coworker who calls an energy drink 'lunch'.
Energy drinks range from 54 to 328 mg of caffeine per 16 fluid ounces (FDA), about six times apart. You can feel caffeine within about 15 minutes, it's absorbed within about 45, and with a half-life of about five hours, half is still in you five hours later. Too much can mean jitters, a racing heart and lost sleep. The FDA cites 400 mg a day for most adults, and medical experts advise against energy drinks for children and teens. A preliminary 2026 AHA conference abstract (not peer-reviewed) found heart events mentioned more often in FDA adverse-event reports involving caffeine and stimulant products; it shows an association, not proof, and not your personal risk. Questions about your heart? See a doctor.

2026-11-16-body-03.description:
Send this to the friend who swears the urge to breathe means you're out of oxygen.
The urge to breathe is driven mainly by carbon dioxide building up, not by oxygen running low: sensors near your brainstem pick up the acid CO2 makes, and your diaphragm starts moving on its own. Oxygen only drives breathing hard when it gets very low, which is why breath-holding in water is dangerous: you can black out without any warning (also called shallow water or hypoxic blackout). The CDC warns that underwater breath-holding games can kill even strong swimmers. Never play them. Questions about your breathing? See a doctor.

2026-11-24-body-01.description:
Send this to the friend whose eye has been twitching all week.
That flutter is eyelid myokymia: the eyelid muscle firing on its own (AAO EyeWiki: up to 3-8 times a second), most often in the lower lid, from a nervous-system glitch. Cleveland Clinic says it's extremely common, usually harmless, and most cases go away within days or weeks. Common triggers: poor sleep, caffeine, stress, eye strain and long screen time. See an eye doctor if it hasn't gone after a few weeks, spreads to other parts of your face, or affects your vision (right away for any vision change).
